title: Data types & collection
examples: What is the difference between discrete and continuous data?
When should I use primary data instead of secondary data?
Can you give an example of a bad question for a survey?

explain.say: Today we learn about different kinds of data. Data is information we collect for study. Knowing the type helps us analyze it correctly.
Discrete data can only take whole number values. Think about counting things that cannot be split apart. For example, the number of students in a class is discrete.
Continuous data can take any value within a range. These measurements can have fractions or decimals. For instance, the height of a person is continuous.
Primary data means you collected it yourself for your study. This is like doing your own survey. Secondary data is information someone else has already collected. Using existing data saves time.
When designing a questionnaire, your questions must be clear. Avoid questions that have two meanings. For example, asking 'Are you happy?' is too vague.

draw.text: Questionnaires: Keep questions clear and specific

faq.q: What is the difference between discrete and continuous data?
faq.a: Discrete data comes from counting things, so it must be a whole number. Continuous data comes from measuring things, so it can have decimals.
asks: Can I count time as discrete?

faq.q: When should I use primary data instead of secondary data?
faq.a: You should use primary data when the existing data does not answer your specific research question. Secondary data is great for background information.
asks: Is it always better to collect new data?
What if the secondary data is old?

faq.q: How do I know if a question on a survey is biased?
faq.a: A biased question pushes you toward a certain answer. Always ask questions that allow for neutral responses.
asks: How do I make a question neutral?

faq.q: Can I mix discrete and continuous data in one study?
faq.a: Yes, you often can. For example, you might count the number of cars (discrete) and measure their average speed (continuous).
asks: Are both types of data okay together?
What if I measure two different things?

faq.q: Does the source of data change its type?
faq.a: No, the source only tells you if it is primary or secondary. The nature of the data—counting or measuring—determines if it is discrete or continuous.
asks: If I measure something, is it always continuous?

facts: Discrete data results from counting items, like the number of pets.
Continuous data results from measuring things, like temperature or time.
Primary data is information gathered directly by the researcher.
Secondary data is information already collected by someone else.
Good questionnaire questions are unbiased and clear.

quiz.say: The number of siblings a person has is an example of:
quiz.why: Because you count whole people, the answer must be a whole number.

wrong.0: This is tempting because some people think all counts are measurements.
wrong.1: This confuses the type of data with where the data came from.
wrong.2: This confuses the type of data with whether it was already collected.

quiz.say: A student measures the time it takes to run one lap. This data is:
quiz.why: Time can be measured to many decimal places, so it is continuous.

wrong.1: This is tempting because we often round time to whole seconds.
wrong.2: This confuses the type of data with the collection method.
wrong.3: This suggests the data was already available, which is not necessarily true.

quiz.say: If you use census data about last year's population, this is:
quiz.why: Census data was collected by a government, not by you for this specific study.

wrong.1: This assumes you had to collect the data yourself for your project.
wrong.2: Population counts are whole numbers, making them discrete, not continuous.
wrong.3: This relates to question wording, not the source of the data.
